full_judgment:
3. The case of the respondents, who were plaintiffs in Title suit No. 436 of 1956, is that Respondents no. 1 and 2 are owners of properties in West Bengal India. The appellants had some building within the Municipal area of Khulna town; Both parties agreed to transfer their properties and agreed to exchange their properties by a devise of permanent lease, each exchanging by a lease deed in favour of the other. Both parties executed to contract for the purpose. One was executed by the appellants in respect of their Khulna Town properties on August 4, 1951 in favour of the respondents M. A. Sabur and his minor daughter Hosne Ara Begum, and the other containing substantially the same provisions was executed by M.A. Sabour for self and as legal guardian of his minor daughter Hosne Ara in respect of their properties in West Bengal, India. The respondents were put into possession of the property in Khulna in pursuance of the said contract. 

 1. In view of section 75A of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. 1950 the contract has become unenforceable as contemplated in sections 23 and S6 of the Contract Act, and as such the suit is liable to be dismissed as not maintainable. 

 3. Consideration of the agreement that is the properties belonging to M. A. Sabur in West Bengal having been lost to him, there is absence of mutuality in the contract, and as such the contract as contemplated under section 15 of the Specific Relief Act and section 55 of the Contract Act cannot be enforced. 

 7. The learned Single Judge of the High Court Division found that the agreement for lease in question was in substance an agreement to exchange of properties and it was to make complete transfer of title and interest in the properties, and as such section 75A of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act was not attracted. It was also held that by the agreement a vested right was created in favour of the respondents and section 75A being not retrospective did not affect the transaction. It was further held that there was a mutuality and that Mr. Sabur as legal guardian of his minor daughter Hosne Ara could enter into .a valid contract for transfer. It was held that the third point was answered while discussing the first point, and on the fourth point it was held that the Courts below came to a correct decision and that the time was not the essence of contract. On the fifth question it was observed that the failure to prove payment of Tk. 500/- out of Tk. 1700/- will not deprive the Respondents from enforcing the contract. In that view of the matter, both the appeals were dismissed. 

 8. Leave was granted on two limited grounds first, is whether section 75A and 81A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act in the facts and circumstances of the case is attracted, and whether the High Court Division erred in not holding that the contract was an executor contract. 

 10. The relevant findings of the learned Single Judge may be set out; From the terms of the two agreements, it appears that the agreement are something more than a simple agreement for tease. The parties adopted this device for effecting a complete exchange of their properties situated in two independent countries, Mr. T. Ali has rightly pointed out that the agreement (Exhibit D) provides that the second part, is to be given possession in a portion of the property under agreement for lease Similarly the agreement (Exhibit 1A) provides that the first party, namely. M. A Sabur will provide accommodation, to the second party free of rent in a house belonging to M. A. Sabur, in West Bengal. The second party was given the authority to realise monthly rents from the temporary tenants in the G.R. Road property with the right to evict the said temporary tenants either by suit or amicably. The annual rental of Rs. 61/- has been fixed in both the agreements which will be automatically set off against the rental payable by the other party. 

 11. In view of the above findings the learned Single Judge has clearly held that the parties to the contract wanted to exchange the properties for their mutual benefit. The finding set out above gives the character of the contract not as a contract for permanent lease, for a contract for exchange which is another form of sale. Mr. Chowdhury found it difficult to urge the bar of section 75A in view of this finding. In this view of the matter the whole complexion of the question under consideration changes. If the contract in substance is a contract for exchange of property which means a sale or the properties obviously the provision of section 75A or for that matter section 81A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act is Not at all attracted and therefore the second question becomes academic and we do riot propose to embark upon any detailed discussion on the subject.
